text: Private First Class Whitt Lloyd Moreland (March 7, 1930 – May 29, 1951) was a United States Marine who heroically sacrificed his life to save fellow Marines by smothering a hand grenade with his body during the UN May–June 1951 counteroffensive of the Korean War. On May 29, 1951, at Kwagch’i-Dong, Korea, while serving as an intelligence scout attached to Company C, First Battalion, Fifth Marines, First Marine Division (Reinforced), he voluntarily accompanied a rifle platoon in a daring assault against a strongly defended enemy hill position, delivering accurate rifle fire that aided in seizing the objective. After the position was secured, he led a party forward to neutralize an enemy bunker observed 400 meters beyond, moving boldly through a fireswept area and nearly reaching the emplacement when the enemy launched a volley of hand grenades. He kicked several grenades off the ridgeline where they exploded harmlessly, and while attempting to kick away another, slipped and fell near the deadly missile. Recognizing that the sputtering grenade would explode before he could move, he shouted a warning to his comrades, covered the missile with his body, and absorbed the full blast, sacrificing his life to save them. For this action, PFC Moreland was posthumously awarded the United States' highest military decoration — the Medal of Honor — making him the 17th Marine to receive it during the Korean War. Born in Waco, Texas on March 7, 1930, Moreland attended public school in Austin and graduated from Junction High School in 1948, where he played football for two years. He enlisted in the United States Marine Corps in September 1948 for one year, serving in San Diego and Camp Pendleton, California, and later enlisted in the Marine Corps Reserve for six years. On November 30, 1950, he was called to active duty and received advanced training at Camp Pendleton, California. Moreland is buried at Whittington Cemetery in Mount Ida, Arkansas, and there is a monument dedicated to him in Llano, Texas, along with others who served in the war. His decorations include the Medal of Honor with one Campaign Star. The President of the United States, Harry S. Truman, presented the Medal of Honor posthumously for service as cited, stating that Moreland's heroic initiative and valiant spirit of self-sacrifice in the face of certain death reflect the highest credit upon him and the United States Naval Service.
